title: Specimen Labeling, Hemolysis, and Needle Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Label laboratory specimens at the bedside using two patient identifiers and complete, legible labels.
- Prevent hemolysis by applying correct collection, mixing, transfer, and transport technique.
- Apply needle safety and disposal practices, including no recapping and point-of-use sharps disposal.
- Recognize hemolyzed, unlabeled, or mislabeled specimens and escalate for correct handling and recollection.
- Recognize the assistant's supervised, policy-following role and escalate out-of-scope or uncertain situations to licensed staff.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of a label like a nametag on a backpack. A good nametag has the person's name and something else that is unique to them — like their birthday — so two kids named 'Sam' don't get mixed up.

### Question 2

It is like writing your name on your cup at a party the moment you set it down — if you wait and do all the cups later, nobody knows whose drink is whose.

### Question 3

It is like tagging a suitcase before it goes on the airport belt — once it is mixed in with the others, it is too late to be sure which one is yours.

### Question 4

A label is like a homework heading — it needs your name, the date, and who wrote it, so the teacher (or lab) knows whose work it is.

### Question 5

It is like putting your friend's name on a lunch box before you know whose lunch is going in — you might hand the wrong lunch to the wrong person.

### Question 6

If you realize you forgot your name sticker, stay right where you are, grab the sticker, and stick it on before the tube ever leaves the room.

### Question 7

If a package arrives with no name on it, you cannot safely give it to anyone — it has to be thrown away and the sender tries again.

### Question 8

Even if someone is napping, you can still read their name tag — you don't need them to talk to know who they are.

### Question 9

If two nametags don't match, you don't guess — you go ask the grown-up in charge to sort it out.

### Question 10

A room number is like a locker number — it tells you the spot, not the person using it, and people move around.

### Question 11

If you are filling several water bottles for one person, you write their name on each bottle as you fill it, not all at the end.

### Question 12

If two people's test scores get swapped, the wrong student could fail or get medicine they don't need — that is how serious a switched label can be.

### Question 13

It is like writing the time on a timed test — the exact time matters, so you fill it in correctly rather than making one up.

### Question 14

When two classmates have the same name, the teacher uses their birthdays or student numbers to tell them apart — the label needs the same trick.

### Question 15

It is like a lifeguard checking your swim band before you go in the water — it is for your own safety, and if you say no, the lifeguard gets help rather than guessing.

### Question 16

It is like: check the person's name, pour the cup, write the name on it right away, then carry it off — in that order, every time.

### Question 17

No matter which school your lunch gets sent to, it still needs your name written on it before it leaves you.

### Question 18

Use a marker that won't wash off, like writing on a water bottle that might sit in a cooler — not something you can wipe away.

### Question 19

Scanning is like the cashier beeping your items and your loyalty card so the computer matches them automatically — but they still double-check.

### Question 20

If you find a nameless cup, you don't guess whose it is — you tell the person in charge and get a fresh one with a name.

### Question 21

If a teammate says 'we'll name the cups later,' the safe teammate says 'let's name them right now so nobody gets the wrong one.'

### Question 22

The name goes on the cup, not just on the tray — because the cup can get separated from the tray.

### Question 23

It is like writing the time on a weather reading — the number only makes sense if you know when it was measured.

### Question 24

If a cup has no name AND the drink is spoiled, you throw it away and start over — you don't guess and serve it.

### Question 25

If the name sticker starts to fall off your cup, you stick a fresh one on right away — you don't peel it off and hope people guess.

### Question 26

It is like a relay race — everyone carries the baton, but the runner holding it right now has to make sure it isn't dropped.

### Question 27

A baby can't tell you their name, so you read their hospital bracelet and check with their grown-up — just like checking a baby's name tag at daycare.

### Question 28

If the order slip and the cup don't match, you stop and ask the person in charge — you don't just pick one and hope it works.

### Question 29

Hemolysis is when the red cells — the tiny red balloons in blood — pop open and leak their red color into the liquid.

### Question 30

If the liquid part of the blood looks pink or red like it was dyed, that usually means the red cells popped — like red juice leaking into clear water.

### Question 31

Shaking a blood tube hard is like shaking a can of soda and popping the bubbles — except here the red cells are the ones that pop.

### Question 32

Pushing blood too hard through a thin straw is like squeezing a water balloon through a keyhole — the pressure makes it burst.

### Question 33

Leaving a rubber band on too long is like a traffic jam in the arm — blood backs up and the sample gets squeezed and changed.

### Question 34

You let hand sanitizer dry before touching things, and the same rule applies here — wet alcohol can drip into the tube and pop the red cells.

### Question 35

Mix blood like you would gently turn a snow globe over a few times — not like you're trying to make whipped cream.

### Question 36

Squeezing a thick milkshake through a tiny straw takes so much force that it gets all beaten up — blood cells get beaten up the same way.

### Question 37

Red cells are like tiny bags full of a chemical called potassium — when the bags pop, the potassium spills out and makes the number look too high.

### Question 38

If the juice is spoiled, you don't serve it and hope nobody notices — you pour a fresh cup.

### Question 39

If you drop the cupcake before it gets to the oven, that's a 'before-baking' problem — hemolysis is the same kind of 'before-testing' problem.

### Question 40

If a package looks damaged when it arrives, you set it aside and tell someone — you don't open it and pretend it is fine.

### Question 41

There are two kinds of popped cells: ones that popped inside the body because of illness, and ones you accidentally popped by shaking too hard after the draw.

### Question 42

Carry the blood like you'd carry a fragile glass of juice — upright, steady, and out of the hot sun or freezer.

### Question 43

Pour the juice slowly into the cup instead of blasting it through a tiny straw — gentle pouring keeps it from foaming up.

### Question 44

Blood is alive for a little while after it's drawn — if it sits too long, the cells get tired and start to break down, like fruit left on the counter.

### Question 45

Bubbles in the blood tube are like bubbles from pouring soda too hard — they mean it was handled too roughly, and the red cells may have popped.

### Question 46

We wait so the cleaning wipe dries — like waiting for hand sanitizer to dry — so none of it drips into the tube and pops the red cells.

### Question 47

If the red bags popped and spilled their potassium, the reading looks high even if the person is fine — so you check again with a fresh sample.

### Question 48

The tube is like a recipe that needs the exact amount of liquid for the powder inside — too little or too much and the recipe goes wrong.

### Question 49

Gentle turning is safe; shaking, forcing, and squeezing are the things that pop the red cells.

### Question 50

If you have to poke around a lot to get the straw in the juice box, the drink gets messy — the same happens to blood with a rough draw.

### Question 51

If a cup gets ruined, you comfort the person, throw the bad one away, and kindly get a fresh cup — you don't blame them or serve the ruined drink.

### Question 52

Freezing whole blood is like putting a water balloon in the freezer — the ice expands and bursts it.

### Question 53

Red cells also carry another chemical called LDH — when the cells pop, that spills out too, so both potassium and LDH look higher than they really are.

### Question 54

On a hot day you wouldn't leave milk in the sun — blood needs the same care to stay good on the way to the lab.

### Question 55

If the red balloons pop before they are counted, the counter gets the number wrong — so a CBC on a popped sample can't be trusted.

### Question 56

If the juice is ruined twice even when you pour it carefully, maybe the problem isn't how you poured it — you tell the grown-up to look closer.

### Question 57

Once a needle is used, it goes straight into the special strong box — you don't try to put its cap back on, because that's when fingers get poked.

### Question 58

It's like trying to put a lid on a sharp pencil while your other hand is right under the point — one slip and you poke yourself.

### Question 59

A used needle goes straight into the strong sharps box right where you're standing — not on the table, not in the trash, not in your pocket.

### Question 60

The sharps box is like a heavy, locked mailbox for needles — strong, sealed, and clearly marked 'careful, sharp things inside.'

### Question 61

When the sharp box is about three-quarters full, you close it and get a new one — like taking out the trash before it overflows, but way more careful.

### Question 62

Twisting or snapping a needle is like snapping a pencil under pressure — it can fly or slip and poke someone, and it might flick blood.

### Question 63

Right after you're done, flip the safety cover on — like putting the guard back on a sharp tool — then drop it in the sharps box.

### Question 64

If a rule book says you must put the cap back, there's a trick to do it with one hand so your other hand stays safely out of the way.

### Question 65

A seatbelt and airbag are 'machine' protections (engineering controls); driving carefully is a 'behavior' protection (work-practice control).

### Question 66

The biohazard sign is the 'beware — sharp and germy inside' sticker that keeps everyone safe.

### Question 67

If you stuff a box so full the sharp points poke out the top, the next person to reach near it gets poked.

### Question 68

If you get poked, wash it with soap and water right away and tell the person in charge — just like telling an adult when you get a splinter.

### Question 69

If you find a needle on the floor, you don't grab it — you use a grabber tool or tell someone trained to pick it up safely.

### Question 70

These are like self-capping pens — after one use the point hides away so it can't poke anyone and can't be used again.

### Question 71

If the trash can is right next to you, you throw it away right there — you don't carry it across the room where you could drop it.

### Question 72

Needles never go in the regular trash, even wrapped up — they always go in the special strong box.

### Question 73

Broken glass is like a dropped plate — you use a broom and dustpan to clean it up, not your hands, and it goes in the sharp-safe box.

### Question 74

The boss has to give workers the safe tools, the strong box, the lessons, and the free hepatitis B shot — it's the workplace rule.

### Question 75

The sharp box sits right where you're working, like a trash can by your desk, so you don't have to walk anywhere with a needle.

### Question 76

An airbag helps in a crash, but you still have to buckle up and drive carefully — the device works only if you use it right.

### Question 77

You can't tell if a cup is dirty just by looking at it — so every spill gets treated and reported the same careful way.

### Question 78

You never put your hand in the sharp box — if it's full, you close it and start a new one, full stop.

### Question 79

If you haven't been trained to do something that pokes a needle into a person, you say no and get someone who is trained to do it.

### Question 80

The assistant is the helper who sets up, labels, and carries the sample — while the trained clinician does the poking and reads the answers.

### Question 81

If you're not sure the name is right, you ask the person in charge — you don't guess and you don't scribble a different name.

### Question 82

Different places have different rules about what helpers can do — like how the rules of a game change depending on which field you're playing on.

### Question 83

If the same player keeps dropping the ball, you tell the coach so everyone can practice — you don't pretend the drops didn't happen.

### Question 84

Before you touch anything with blood or needles, you need the lesson, the rule book, and the go-ahead from the person in charge.

### Question 85

Do it in order: check the name, draw, label right away, mix gently, drop the needle in the sharp box, then carry it off — every safety rule in one smooth routine.
